emailSubject: FMB News | US Formally Requests Extradition of Apollo Quiboloy; DFA Transmits Demand to DOJ | August 7, 2026 | 12:00 AM PHT
headline: DOJ Begins Review of US Extradition Request for Apollo Quiboloy
kicker: Justice · Extradition · Philippines and United States
deck: The Department of Justice has begun evaluating the United States’ formal request to extradite Apollo Quiboloy, while his Philippine criminal cases remain pending.
author: FMB News Desk

sections.heading: What happened
paragraphs: The Department of Justice has begun evaluating the United States’ formal request to extradite detained Kingdom of Jesus Christ founder Apollo Quiboloy after the Department of Foreign Affairs transmitted the request to the department.

sections.heading: What we know
paragraphs: Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida said the review will consider the Philippines-US extradition treaty, relevant Philippine laws and rules, Supreme Court decisions and Quiboloy’s pending local cases.

A 2021 federal indictment in California charges Quiboloy and several associates with alleged offenses that include sex trafficking of children, labor trafficking, visa fraud, bulk cash smuggling and money laundering.

Quiboloy was arrested by Philippine authorities in September 2024 and remains in Philippine custody while facing separate domestic cases, including qualified human trafficking and child-abuse charges.

The accusations remain allegations unless proven in court. Quiboloy has denied wrongdoing. His lawyer has argued that extradition would face legal obstacles, while the DOJ said it would conduct its own evaluation.

sections.heading: Background
paragraphs: The Philippines and the United States are parties to a bilateral extradition treaty signed in 1994. The treaty and Philippine extradition law require the DOJ to assess the request before prosecutors may ask a Philippine court to approve extradition.

The treaty also contains a temporary-surrender mechanism that may apply when a requested person is already facing proceedings in the requested country. Whether that mechanism can or should be used in this case will be determined through the Philippine legal process.

sections.heading: What remains unclear
paragraphs: It remains unclear when the DOJ will complete its assessment, whether it will file an extradition petition, and how Quiboloy’s pending Philippine cases will affect the timing or form of any court action.

sections.heading: Why this matters
paragraphs: The case tests how Philippine courts balance domestic criminal proceedings, treaty obligations, national jurisdiction, and the interests of alleged victims in two countries. Extradition is a judicial process, not an automatic transfer ordered by either government.

sections.heading: What happens next
paragraphs: The DOJ will finish its legal and factual evaluation before deciding whether to pursue an extradition petition in a Philippine court. Extradition is not automatic, and Quiboloy may contest any petition through the judicial process.
